articles.title: What tarot showed me was not "an unknown future," but "my true feelings, not yet put into words"
articles.summary: Do you think of tarot cards as something mysterious — something that can tell you about a fate or future you don't know yourself?

blocks.text: Do you think of tarot cards as something mysterious — something that can tell you about a fate or future you don't know yourself?
I used to think that way, too. I felt a strange pull toward them, as if they had some special power and could hand down an answer from above, one I hadn't noticed myself.
But when you approach tarot through psychology and the process of decision-making, you start to see that what makes it interesting lies somewhere a little different.
Not a prophecy falling from the sky, but an answer already inside you

What tarot brings to light is not a prophecy about a future someone else has decided. It is your own honest feelings — feelings that are already inside you, but that the busyness of daily life and thoughts about how things "should" be have kept you from putting into words.

When we are asked, out of nowhere, "What do you want to do?", we often find ourselves at a loss for an answer. The same thoughts go round and round in our heads, and we tend to land on the same safe conclusion as always.
That is where looking through the filter of a question — the 78 cards — can help.

For example, suppose you draw a card and feel that "somehow, this message doesn't quite sit right with me." In fact, that sense of something not sitting right is the greatest gain of all. Because if you feel that discomfort, it is proof that another answer — "this is what I really want" — already exists inside you.
A time to meet a part of yourself you didn't know

The hope that you might learn something you don't know about yourself is half right, and half a little off. It is not that you learn about a completely unrelated future. It is that you encounter thoughts deep within yourself — "I had no idea I felt this way."
DECIDE. is a web service where you can have that kind of dialogue with yourself in a quiet space, without leaning too far into the spiritual.

You draw a single card on a screen stripped of unnecessary decoration, and as you read the hint for when you're unsure that comes with it, you gradually sort out your thoughts. By the time you finish, the fog in your head has somehow cleared, and what to do next becomes clear.
Why not start by reflecting what's in your head right now, as if you were going to meet a part of yourself you didn't know?

articles.title: What to do when a "bad card" comes up in tarot? A new way to relate to the cards, for those who tend to feel anxious
articles.summary: You may be a little curious about tarot, but worry that if an ominous image or a card with a bad meaning came up, you would dwell on it all day. So you keep your distance without quite knowing why. I think there are quite a few people like that.

blocks.text: You may be a little curious about tarot, but worry that if an ominous image or a card with a bad meaning came up, you would dwell on it all day. So you keep your distance without quite knowing why. I think there are quite a few people like that.

It is only natural that the more serious you are, and the more deeply you tend to think things over, the more careful you are about being confronted with negative words. There is no need to go out of your way to experience that sinking feeling you get when a morning horoscope puts you in last place, is there?
But what if, in tarot, there is no such thing as a "good" or "bad" result in the first place?
Scary cards are a catalog of perspectives that give you a calm brake

Originally, the 78 tarot cards are like a "catalog of perspectives" that covers patterns of human thought and situations. Even the cards that seem "scary" or "bad" at first glance are not there to frighten you. They simply offer a calm brake, a perspective for reviewing things — "if you watch out for this risk or oversight right now, things may go better."

For example, suppose a card comes up that suggests returning a plan to a blank slate. Instead of taking it as "I'm destined to fail," try using it as objective advice: "Let me pause and check whether there's anything unreasonable about my current approach." Seen that way, it stops being something to fear at all.
So the result doesn't sway you — and you stay in control
DECIDE., a decision-support service I have recently come to enjoy using, embodies exactly this way of using tarot — one that isn't scary and doesn't sway you.

This service has no eerie staging designed to make people anxious, and no definitive pronouncements. Whichever card you draw, all you will find there are forward-looking, thoughtful hints for when you're unsure, about how to view your current situation and how to move.

Rather than letting a card decide your fate and swinging between joy and disappointment, you use the card as a starting point to choose an answer you can feel satisfied with yourself. The control is always with you, not the card.
I hope that people who don't like being swayed by fortune-telling results will try this quiet, gentle time for organizing their thoughts.

articles.title: You don't need to memorize all 78 meanings. How to use tarot as a tool for organizing your thoughts, starting from zero knowledge
articles.summary: When you think about trying tarot cards for yourself, isn't the first hurdle you run into the daunting idea that you have to memorize the meanings of all 78 cards?

blocks.text: When you think about trying tarot cards for yourself, isn't the first hurdle you run into the daunting idea that you have to memorize the meanings of all 78 cards?

Between the Major Arcana and the Minor Arcana, and upright and reversed positions on top of that, the combinations are enormous. I often hear stories of people who bought a thick guidebook, only to close it partway through because the explanations of history and symbolism were too complicated.
But if your purpose is to organize your own thoughts or get a hint for everyday choices, there is no need at all to memorize the meanings of the cards.
No one memorizes the whole dictionary before using it

When we look something up in a dictionary, none of us memorizes the entire dictionary first. Each time, we look up the word we need and check its meaning against our own context — and that is enough for it to be useful. Tarot, too, should be allowed to be that light and practical a tool.
What matters is not "knowing the meaning of the card," but the process of reading the hint written there and feeling something in your own mind.
Not studying first, but deepening your thinking as you use it
DECIDE. is a service designed so you can go through that process right away, even with zero knowledge.

When you open your browser and draw a card, the card's essential meaning and a concrete hint for untangling your current uncertainty are shown in refined words that sink in easily. There is no need to look up technical terms, and no time spent flipping through a book.

What's more, you can record the result you drew and what you were thinking at the time as a log, so when you look back later, you can see your own patterns of thought and statistics — "so that's the standard I used to decide back then."

Rather than studying first and using it later, you deepen your own thinking as you use it. When you let go of difficult knowledge, tarot becomes a much closer, more reliable companion for everyday life.

articles.title: For those who doubt that "a card drawn by chance could tell the future": a logical way to use tarot I hope you'll try
articles.summary: Isn't it logically strange to think that a single card drawn at random could have your future or your answer written on it?

blocks.text: Isn't it logically strange to think that a single card drawn at random could have your future or your answer written on it?

I think having that doubt is a very healthy, intelligent response. If someone stated flatly, "This card came up, so your fortune next month will absolutely be like this," I probably wouldn't believe it either.
So why have so many business leaders, creators, and even psychologists, for so long, brought an element of chance like tarot into their decision-making and the organizing of their thoughts?
A chance perspective resets the bias in your thinking
It is not because they believe in the magic of the cards. It is because they know the effect that a random perspective has in shaking up the brain.

When we think with only our own heads, we cannot help but stay trapped within our own framework of past experience and current emotions. It is a state of so-called confirmation bias. So we deliberately bring in an outside perspective that has nothing to do with our own intentions — a card drawn by chance.

For example, suppose that while you are unsure whether to move forward or step back, a card suggesting "rest" or "observation" happens to come up. Your brain then begins to simulate from an angle you hadn't considered before: "What would happen if I chose to do nothing for now?"

In other words, the card is not predicting the future. By using a chance card as a partner to bounce your thoughts off, your own field of vision widens, and as a result you become able to arrive at the conclusion you find most convincing, under your own power. Rather than fortune-telling, this could be called an extremely rational method of brainstorming.
A rational partner to bounce thoughts off, for people who don't believe in fortune-telling
DECIDE. is a service made precisely as a thinking tool for making "decisions you can truly feel satisfied with."

You draw a card not as part of a spiritual debate about whether to believe or not, but as a framework for resetting the bias in your thinking and gaining a new angle. The log and statistics features are also there so you can look back objectively on your own decision-making process.
I especially hope that rational people who don't believe in fortune-telling will try, just once, how comfortable this kind of thought-organizing using chance can feel.

articles.title: For those who think "this isn't a big enough dilemma to ask about": why small, everyday uncertainties are worth not leaving alone
articles.summary: When you hear words like tarot or fortune-telling, you might picture them as something people turn to when they face a life-changing decision, or a serious uncertainty they cannot tell anyone about.

blocks.text: When you hear words like tarot or fortune-telling, you might picture them as something people turn to when they face a life-changing decision, or a serious uncertainty they cannot tell anyone about.
Right now, I do not have anything that urgent weighing on me, so this probably is not something I need.

It is only natural to feel that way. But if we look back at our everyday lives for a moment, even if they do not quite amount to serious worries, there are a surprising number of small uncertainties and things we just cannot quite decide, scattered all around.
How Small Undecided Things in Your Head Create Tiredness

Should I fill my next day off with plans and go out, or take it easy and relax at home?
With the work I have on my plate, should I start with A first, or take my time carefully refining B?
That book or course I have been curious about — should I sign up at this timing?

When we hesitate over small everyday choices like these, we tend to put them off with a vague "well, either way is fine," or just choose out of habit. But when several of these small undecided things pile up in your head, they quietly use up your mental bandwidth and leave you in a state where your head never quite feels clear.
Putting a Satisfying Full Stop to Small Everyday Choices
DECIDE. is not for reading life's biggest moments. It is for putting a full stop — one you can feel good about, in your own way — on these small everyday uncertainties.
You do not need an uncertainty big enough to want a reading. With a light feeling, like "How do I want to approach today?" or "What is this vague unease really about?", try drawing a single card.

Reading the hint written there, you can calmly confirm where you stand right now: "Ah, I am a bit tired at the moment, so what I really wanted was to choose rest." And by keeping a log of the results you chose, you gradually start to see your own patterns of thinking.
Not to solve a big uncertainty, but to turn each small everyday choice into one you truly feel good about. That accumulation is what eventually creates a comfortable daily life with less uncertainty.
Precisely because you do not have a serious uncertainty right now, why not try it lightly, as a new habit for clearing your head?

articles.title: Are you suffering from "decision fatigue"? A new reflection habit to clear your mind at the end of the day
articles.summary: You wake up and choose what to wear, decide what to have for lunch, and work out how to reply to countless emails. It is said that the number of decisions a person makes in a single day runs into the thousands, counting only the ones we are aware of.

blocks.text: You wake up and choose what to wear, decide what to have for lunch, and work out how to reply to countless emails. It is said that the number of decisions a person makes in a single day runs into the thousands, counting only the ones we are aware of.

By night, your head somehow feels heavy, and the important things you really want to think about are the very things you keep putting off. That is not because your will is weak. It is simply because you are suffering from "decision fatigue."
Too many things to think about is what wears your brain out

When we decide something, the part that uses the most energy is the work of searching for "what angle to think from." When you try to produce an answer from zero in front of a blank sheet of paper, your brain starts searching through every possibility and uses up its memory in no time.
That is why, when you are tired, the wise approach is to hand that "framework for thinking" over to something outside yourself.
Use a single card as training wheels for your thoughts
DECIDE., a service I use in the quiet hours of the night, is a thinking tool designed precisely to ease this decision fatigue.

Instead of agonizing from zero, you simply react to the viewpoint presented — "that might be true" or "no, I think differently" — so you can reach how you really feel with surprisingly little energy.
At the end of the day, quietly put away the undecided matters in your head before you go to sleep. Why not start that kind of pleasant habit?

A filter that turns intuition into words
The problem is that this intuition comes out as a vague feeling of "somehow," so even you yourself cannot explain why you thought that way.

articles.title: Upright and reversed are not "good luck" and "bad luck." A thinking exercise for looking evenly at both sides of a situation

blocks.text: Many of you may know that in tarot, a card can appear in its correct orientation, called "upright," or upside down, called "reversed." And generally, when a reversed card appears, it tends to be interpreted as "it takes on a bad meaning" or "your luck is going down."

But when you look at tarot as a tool for decision-making and organizing your thoughts, upright and reversed simply represent the two sides of something, or whether its energy is in excess or in short supply.
The Perspective That a Strength, Taken Too Far, Becomes a Weakness

For example, suppose there is a card that means "strong will and moving forward." If it is working smoothly, it becomes reliable momentum, but if it becomes excessive, it can turn into "running out of control or being self-centered," and if it is lacking, it becomes "indecisiveness."
A reversed position is exactly that — an objective sign that says, "your balance may be a little off here."
A Framework for Seeing a Situation from Many Angles

In DECIDE., no matter which way a card appears, it is not treated as an ominous prediction. It is presented as a calm, thoughtful hint that says, "you could also review the situation from this angle."
Everything has two sides, and behind every benefit there is a hidden risk. Looking at both sides evenly through a single card is a wonderful exercise in thinking that sharpens your everyday judgment.
Why not graduate from fortune-telling that swings you between joy and worry over good and bad luck, and try touching the cards as a tool for seeing things in three dimensions?

blocks.text: At work and in private life, when you have to choose something, there are times when you think "which one is the right answer?" and your feet stop moving. The more you think you do not want to fail or lose out, the more you go back and forth across search screens while only time passes by.
But if you think about it calmly for a moment, since no one can know the future, it is impossible to know the "100% correct answer" before you choose.
Not Choosing the Right Answer, but Making Your Chosen Path the Right One

What matters is not guessing a correct answer that is lying somewhere waiting to be found, but holding your own "answer you can feel good about" — "right now, for these reasons, I chose this." If you choose a path you truly feel good about, even if something unexpected happens along the way, you can adjust course without regret.
The words in DECIDE.'s concept, "Decisions you can truly feel good about," carry exactly that feeling.
Making the Decision-Making Process Visible
With this service, you do not just draw a card and get a hint — you can also keep a "log" of what you were thinking at that time and how you decided.

What the result will be belongs to the future, but the process — how you hesitated, and how you reached a decision you felt good about — is in your own hands right now. I think treating that process with care is itself a skill for living flexibly in an age full of uncertainty.
Why not try finding your own answer — one that will not show up in a search — in this quiet screen?

articles.title: "What I want to do" or "what I should do"? A place to return to when you're torn between two choices

blocks.text: When you boil it down, much of our everyday uncertainty is a tug-of-war between "what I want to do (feelings, my true feelings)" and "what I should do (reason, duty)."

In your heart you want to rest, but should you push yourself to meet the expectations around you? Should you protect your current stable environment, or step out into a new challenge? Precisely because both matter, you cannot easily find an answer and your heart wavers.
Not Forcing a Black-or-White Answer, but Searching for a Third Way
When feelings and reason are clashing, if you try to force a decision by suppressing one side or the other, a backlash always comes later: "I should have chosen the other one after all."
What matters is not cornering yourself with an either-or choice between A and B, but holding a third perspective: "How can I find a point where both sides can feel satisfied?"
How the 78 Cards Show You Ways to Find Balance
When you draw a card in DECIDE., you are presented with a hint for looking at your current situation from a higher viewpoint, one step back.

Reading it, your calm returns, and you can shift the timeline — "First I will finish what I should do now, and start preparing for what I want to do next month" — or set priorities — "I will not give up this part, but I will let go of the rest."
When you feel caught between two feelings, take a deep breath and try listening to the quiet words of a card.

blocks.text: Why have tarot cards continued to be used by people all over the world for hundreds of years, without disappearing? If they were merely some dubious magical item, they should have been weeded out long ago in the course of history.

The reason tarot has survived for so long is that within its 78 cards, every pattern of "emotion, conflict, growth, and human relationships" that people experience in life is systematized with surprising precision.
Overlaying yourself, as you are now, onto a universal story

The elation of starting something new, the stagnation of hitting a wall, the pain of letting something go, and the sense of renewal when you start walking again. No matter how much the times and technology change, the essence of the drama we experience in our hearts does not change.
Tarot is, so to speak, an "encyclopedia of human experience" created by those who came before us.
Classical wisdom, through a modern interface

Rather than confronting you with difficult classical symbolism as it is, it has been rebuilt as refined Japanese hints that people living today can apply directly to choices at work and in daily life.
Why not put the wisdom of the 78 cards to use in your everyday decision-making, with the feeling of opening a fine work of classical literature or philosophy?

In other words, if you regularly treat small choices with care and practice checking in with your true feelings, anyone can raise both the speed and the quality of their decisions.

articles.title: Finding the source of a "vague anxiety." Steps to turn a hazy unease into concrete action
articles.summary: You cannot pinpoint the reason, but somehow your heart feels unsettled. When you think about the future, a vague anxiety washes over you. I think everyone has nights like that.

blocks.text: You cannot pinpoint the reason, but somehow your heart feels unsettled. When you think about the future, a vague anxiety washes over you. I think everyone has nights like that.

It is said that people feel the most stress not when the problem itself is large, but when they "do not know what the problem is (cannot see its outline)." Just as a haunted house is scary because it is dark and you cannot see, anxiety also looks biggest while you do not know what it really is.
Give your unease a tentative name
The first step to calming a vague anxiety is to give that unease concrete words or a theme, and turn on the light in the room.
At times like that, I open DECIDE. and draw one card based on how I am feeling right now.
Once you can see the outline, the next step becomes clear

Suppose, for example, the card you drew has hints written on it such as "concern about not being prepared enough" or "boundaries with the people around you." Then you realize, "Ah, the reason I was somehow anxious was that, in a corner of my mind, I still had not finished preparing for next week's presentation" — and the true nature of the anxiety turns into a concrete task.
Once you know what it really is, you can turn it into a concrete action — "then tomorrow morning, I'll spend just 30 minutes working on the materials" — and your heart grows quiet in an instant.
When you are carrying an unease you cannot explain, try borrowing the light of a card to gently illuminate what is inside your heart.

articles.title: The light way of thinking that saved me when perfectionism left me unable to move: "decide provisionally, for now"
articles.summary: When you try to start something new, you cannot move until every condition is in place and you are certain you will absolutely not fail. Do you struggle with that kind of perfectionist tendency?

blocks.text: When you try to start something new, you cannot move until every condition is in place and you are certain you will absolutely not fail. Do you struggle with that kind of perfectionist tendency?
If you treat decisions too heavily — "once I decide, I have to see it through to the end" or "I must not make the wrong choice" — the first step becomes as heavy as lead.
A Decision Is a Hypothesis You Can Always Revise

To move more lightly, it helps to reframe a decision not as "a fixed matter that can never be changed for life," but as "a provisional decision (a hypothesis) for today, for now." Precisely because you decide provisionally and take a step, new information comes in, and you become able to make the next, better choice.
The thing that gently pushes your back toward that "light provisional decision" is DECIDE..
Comfortably Lowering the Hurdle of a Decision That Feels Too Heavy

It feels painful because you try to carry everything and decide all by yourself. Instead, in a good sense, use the card as a trigger: "Today this card gave me this hint, so I will try going with this approach first."
Of course, if you move and something feels off, you can simply stop at that point and think again. Even that process of trial and error becomes a valuable asset of your own if you keep it as a log.
When you feel your feet might stop from overthinking, why not draw a single card and take a light step forward?

articles.title: So you don't regret "what if I had chosen differently back then." Three conditions for making decisions you can accept
articles.summary: After you have decided something, there are times when the path you did not choose looks sparkling, and you think, "Maybe I should have chosen that one after all." It is the so-called "the grass is always greener on the other side" phenomenon, but why does this regret arise...

blocks.text: After you have decided something, there are times when the path you did not choose looks sparkling, and you think, "Maybe I should have chosen that one after all." It is the so-called "the grass is always greener on the other side" phenomenon, but why does this regret arise?
In many cases, it is not because the result itself was bad, but because in the process of deciding, you had not fully listened to your own true feelings.
Three Steps That Create a Sense of Satisfaction

A decision you will not regret when you look back on it has three conditions. First, do not ignore your own feelings. Second, consider an objective perspective different from your own at least once. And third, hold the sense of agency that, in the end, "I chose this myself."
DECIDE. is a service that lets you naturally trace these three steps in just a few minutes.
If You Follow the Process Carefully, Any Result Becomes Nourishment

First, by drawing a card while being aware of your own uncertainty, you face your true feelings. Next, you read the objective hint the card presents and broaden your view. And finally, you reach a conclusion by your own intention and record it in a log.
If an answer comes through this careful process, even if difficulties come afterward, you can keep trusting yourself: "That was the path my past self chose, doing the best I could at the time."
To build up choices without regret, why not try valuing the decision-making process itself?

Even though you know this, when you are in the middle of an emotional whirlpool, your field of vision narrows with the thought "I have to do something right now," and you are tempted to act impulsively.
A system for inserting a pause before you decide
An effective way to prevent such impulsive judgments is to physically insert a few minutes of a "cool-down ritual" before you decide something or press the send button.
For me, the action that plays that role is drawing one card with DECIDE.
Objective words cool down a heated head

When my heart feels unsettled, I open the screen, draw one card, and slowly read the text written there in its calm tone. In those tens of seconds to a few minutes, I feel my breathing deepen, strangely enough, and the wave of emotion gradually recede.
By coming into contact with the objective viewpoint the card offers, I can regain my calm self and think, "Right now, instead of rushing to a conclusion, I'll sleep on it and think tomorrow."
As a gentle brake to protect yourself, why not keep a quiet conversation partner in your pocket at all times?

Your eye naturally settles on the part you are concerned about

A barometer that reflects your current condition

Why not enjoy your dialogue with the cards as a mirror that reflects your heart, which changes little by little every day?

Even doing the same work, whether you feel "I am being made to do this" or "I am choosing to do this myself" makes a complete difference to how fulfilled your heart feels.
From Days Swept Along, to Days You Choose Yourself
That said, in a busy daily life, you tend to get swept along by the pace around you and by habit, and the day ends before you are even aware of what you are choosing.
That is exactly why it matters to have time, in small everyday moments, to consciously place a punctuation mark: "This is what I thought, and this is what I decided."
A Ritual, Once a Day, to Confirm Your Own Will

Drawing a card with DECIDE., organizing your thoughts while reading the hint, and leaving it in a log. This series of simple actions is a small but rich ritual for taking back into your own hands the "sense of self-determination" that is so easily lost.

It does not have to be a big decision. "Deciding in a way I feel good about" today's way of spending the day, or the small choice in front of you. That accumulation should turn your everyday life into something more solid and more comfortable.

articles.title: Make choices your self a year from now can be proud of. A new habit for turning daily uncertainties and decisions into an "asset"

Don't you think that is a little wasteful?
The process of being unsure itself becomes wisdom that is yours alone

Whether it was a decision that went well or one that turned out a little bittersweet, if you have a record of how you thought at the time and what hint gave you the push to take a step forward, all of it becomes an "asset" that will help your future self.
That is why DECIDE. values its log and statistics features, rather than being just a card-drawing tool.
A logbook of your thoughts, as a gift to your future self

The one decision you arrived at today, after feeling unsure and talking with the hints from a card. Quietly recording it is like leaving a letter for yourself one year from now: "Back then, I thought this seriously and chose this path."
Feeling unsure is never a sign of weakness. It is precisely because we are trying to live better that we feel unsure.
Why not turn that precious time of uncertainty, instead of simply consuming it, into a solid record that will support your life from here on?

articles.title: On nights when "the road not taken" looks dazzling. Organizing your thoughts so the grass on the other side doesn't steal your heart
articles.summary: After a big purchase, after choosing a work project, or even after deciding how to spend a day off, have you ever felt that the option you did not choose suddenly looks brighter, thinking "if I had chosen that one, might it have been more fun?" — the choice...

blocks.text: After a big purchase, after choosing a work project, or even after deciding how to spend a day off, have you ever felt that the option you did not choose suddenly looks brighter, thinking "if I had chosen that one, might it have been more fun?"

In psychology, this is called "post-decision dissonance." Because choosing one thing also means letting go of other possibilities at the same time, the brain unconsciously overestimates "the value of what was lost."
Shining Light Not on the Option You Let Go, but on Your Reason for Choosing

The reason the path you did not choose looks dazzling is not that it was truly better — it is simply that "because you have not experienced it yet, you can inflate convenient imaginings about it as much as you like."
What you need on a night like that is to stop gazing at someone else's grass, and do the work of remembering once again the sense of satisfaction you had at the start: "Why did I choose this path?"
Looking Back at Your Log, You Can Meet Your True Feelings from That Time
The biggest reason I use DECIDE. to record my everyday choices may be exactly this — to prevent the "sway back after choosing."

When you are uncertain, draw a single card, and keep a log of the process you thought through using its hint as a clue. Later, when your heart wavers — "maybe the other one was better" — and you open that log, the warmth of your past self comes back to you: "That's right, at that time I wanted to avoid this risk and prioritize this comfort, and I decided it myself."
The present you properly affirming the conclusion your past self reached after thinking seriously. That repetition creates a sense of security that does not waver, no matter which path you choose.

articles.title: You can't prioritize because "everything matters." A process of subtraction to clear the traffic jam in your head
articles.summary: When the things you have to do are piling up, business books and the like invariably say, "First, let's set priorities." But when you actually open a notepad, everything looks important, and you cannot put them in order — isn't that how it honestly feels...

blocks.text: When the things you have to do are piling up, business books and the like invariably say, "First, let's set priorities." But when you actually open a notepad, everything looks important, and you cannot put them in order — isn't that how it honestly feels?
Work, time with family, your own health, learning as a hobby — precisely because all of them are important elements, we lose sight of what to start with and end up standing still.
From an Additive Schedule to Subtractive Choices
What you need when your head is jammed is not to think "which one should I make number one," but a subtractive perspective: "What can I, right now, temporarily set aside?"
Thinking only inside your own head, you tend to become greedy: "I cannot let go of any of this." So I draw a single card in DECIDE. and pass things through an objective filter.
Deciding What Not to Do, Using the Card's Hint as a Criterion

For example, if the card you drew suggests "focus" or "solidifying the foundations," I boldly entrust the other tasks to next week's me: "All right, this week I will not expand into new projects — I will just carefully finish the work right in front of me."

No one can do everything perfectly at the same time. Once you become able to do that quiet subtraction — "now I choose this, and I do not choose that" — the noise in your head disappears, and your body starts to move with surprising lightness.

articles.title: A discomfort you can't put into words is an important signal from within. How to notice your unease instead of ignoring it
articles.summary: The conditions are not bad, and the people around you agree. Logically, it is a situation where you should say "yes," yet for some reason your chest feels unsettled and you cannot nod honestly. Have you had that experience?

blocks.text: The conditions are not bad, and the people around you agree. Logically, it is a situation where you should say "yes," yet for some reason your chest feels unsettled and you cannot nod honestly. Have you had that experience?

In the past, I would force down small discomforts like that with logic — "it must be my imagination" or "I should not be asking for too much" — and move forward, and I often ended up carrying great tiredness and regret afterward.
Not Leaving a Feeling That Cannot Be Put into Words As It Is

Just because you cannot explain the reason does not mean that discomfort is wrong. Rather, your logical thinking simply has not caught up yet, and your senses are sounding the alarm early: "Something is out of line with my values."
However, that alarm has no words, so finding out what it is sounding for takes a little ingenuity.
Using the 78 Cards as a Mirror to Find What It Really Is
At times like that, I open DECIDE. and draw a single card. I use the "hint for when you are uncertain" shown there as a "mirror" for my own discomfort.

While reading the hint, there are moments when the true shape of the unease appears clearly in words: "Ah, I thought the conditions were good, but I was feeling stifled by this part — that my freedom would decrease."
A small discomfort is an important sensor for you to be yourself. Instead of pretending not to see it, try listening carefully to its voice in this quiet screen.

blocks.text: You can't say no when someone asks you for something, and when there's an interesting invitation, you end up packing your schedule. The more responsible and curious a person is, the more likely they are to find their calendar with no blank space at all, and one day tire out as if a thread had snapped.
What we truly need "decisiveness" for may be less when starting something new, and more in the moments when we decide, "I won't do this now," or "From here on, I'll let this go."
Letting go is not running away, but a strategic choice
When we decline or stop something, we tend to feel guilty. But with both hands full, we cannot receive the truly important things that will come our way.
When it feels painful to decide to "stop" by my own will alone, I rely on DECIDE. as a partner for my thinking.
An objective perspective gives you a push to let go

Among the 78 tarot cards, there are many that speak of the importance of "rest," "completion," and "setting down your load." When you encounter those cards in DECIDE., the words reach you not as mere comfort, but as a thoughtful hint: "To move on to what's next, creating space now is the most rational decision."
Reading that, you become able to forgive yourself, thinking, "Resting and declining are also fine decisions for moving forward."
Before you take everything on yourself, why not pause once and look for which of the loads you are carrying now you could set down?

articles.title: For Sunday nights, when the coming week feels a little heavy. A five-minute weekend reset to bring your mind back to neutral
articles.summary: From Sunday evening into the night, your heart somehow feels heavy, and the arrival of Monday morning feels like a burden. Do you spend the end of the weekend like that?

blocks.text: From Sunday evening into the night, your heart somehow feels heavy, and the arrival of Monday morning feels like a burden. Do you spend the end of the weekend like that?

The true nature of that gloom is that you imagine the hardships that might happen next week as "one huge lump all together." It is a state where, on Sunday night, you borrow in advance and carry a whole week's worth of pressure that has not even begun yet.
Loosening the Lump of One Week and Regaining Your Own Pace
The trick to welcoming Monday lightly is not just checking next week's schedule, but deciding just one theme of your own: "How do I want to feel as I spend next week?"
On Sunday nights, I brew herbal tea or coffee and cherish the time I spend opening DECIDE..
Giving Next Week's You a Perspective Like a Protective Charm

On the quiet screen, I draw a single card and slowly read the hint attached to it. For example, if a message like "rely on those around you" or "do not aim for perfection" appears, I simply make it my slogan for next week.

Just by settling your heart — "Next week, I will make it a week where I consult those around me instead of carrying everything alone" — the vague anxiety about Monday changes into concrete actions you can control yourself.
Before you are swallowed by busy everyday life, why not create five minutes on the weekend to return your heart to a flat, even place?

articles.title: It's okay not to have a big dream or goal. Small choices about "how to spend today" eventually shape the outline of a life
articles.summary: In the world of career design and self-development, people often say, "Let's set goals for five years from now" or "Let's clarify your life vision." Of course, having goals is wonderful, but when you cannot find them...

blocks.text: In the world of career design and self-development, people often say, "Let's set goals for five years from now" or "Let's clarify your life vision." Of course, having goals is wonderful, but when you cannot find them, do you ever feel anxious and think, "Maybe I have no core of my own"?
But drawing a blueprint of the distant future is not the only way to design a life.
Living Not by Working Back from the Future, but by Building Up from Today

There is a way of living where you decide the distant mountaintop and climb by the shortest distance, and there is also a way of living where you walk the path in front of you today, step by step, savoring it — "the view this way seems more comfortable" — and before you know it, you have arrived at a place that fits you perfectly.
In the latter way of living, what matters most is "choosing the small choice right in front of you now, without lying to your own true feelings."
Carefully Collecting Small Everyday Satisfactions
DECIDE. is a service that stays close to exactly those people who value "building up from today."

Not a grand life consultation, but for everyday choices like "With what attitude should I face work this afternoon?" or "Which friend should I contact this weekend?", you draw a card, choose the way your heart moves, and leave it in a log.
When many of those small points of satisfaction gather together, looking back, they have become a beautiful trajectory that belongs to no one but you.

articles.title: When a past failure crosses your mind and you can't take a step. How to separate "who I was then" from "who I am now"

blocks.text: When you face a new challenge, or try to take a relationship with someone one step further, do you ever feel your feet freeze as a bitter memory from the past raises its head: "But I failed at something similar before"?
Because the brain has a defensive instinct to protect us from getting hurt, it strongly remembers past failure data and applies the brakes: "If you do the same thing, you will get hurt again."
Even If the Situation Is Similar, You Yourself Have Already Changed
But if you think about it calmly, the you who failed in the past and the you who is here today should be completely different in experience, in the environment around you, and in depth of thinking.
To remove the filter of past memories and look evenly at "how can I move, as I am now?", I draw a card in DECIDE..
With a New Perspective, the Same Result Will Not Repeat

The objective hint a card presents teaches you a "new angle" that is not on the extension of the past. "That time I failed because I rushed ahead on momentum alone, but as this card's hint says, this time if I share things carefully in advance, it should go well" — concrete countermeasures come into view.
A past failure is not a chain that binds you — it is simply valuable reference material for doing better this time.
When you feel an old memory dragging at your feet, why not draw one new perspective and take a step forward with the strength you have now?

articles.title: Why we're good at advising others, but hesitate over ourselves. Tips for seeing yourself objectively, "as if you were someone else"

blocks.text: When a friend or a junior colleague consults you, you can organize things clearly and advise, "You should do it this way." But when it comes to your own uncertainty, your vision suddenly clouds over and you no longer know what to do. Have you experienced that strange phenomenon?

This is called "Solomon's paradox" in psychology: when it comes to ourselves, emotions and calculations of gain and loss become too entangled, and we become unable to bring out the wisdom we actually have.
How to view your own uncertainty from one seat away

Conversely, even with your own uncertainty, if you can view it from a little distance, "as if a dear friend had consulted you about it," you can use the wisdom you already have to arrive at an answer smoothly.
As a device that instantly creates that "psychological distance," DECIDE. works excellently.
By placing a card in between, you can become a calm observer

When you are worrying inside your own head alone, the problem and you are stuck tightly together. But when you open DECIDE.'s screen, draw one card, and read the text written there, a viewpoint is born that lets you look at your uncertainty from outside, as "a theme on the screen."

While reading the card's hints, try thinking, "If a friend drew this card in the same situation, what would I say to them?" Then, surprisingly kind and rational conclusions come out of your own mouth.
If you tend to get lost in a labyrinth when it comes to your own matters, please try this tool for viewing things objectively.

Continuously taking in a large amount of passively flowing information and other people's emotions drains our brain's energy more than we realize.
From time spent soaking up "outside information" to time spent listening to your "inner voice"

Of course, it is not realistic to completely let go of your smartphone in modern life. That is why, even when you are looking at the same screen, I recommend gradually replacing "time spent passively watching other people's posts" with "active time spent organizing your own thoughts."
As a switch for that change, I keep DECIDE. on my smartphone's home screen.
A noise-free screen brings your scattered attention back

Why not start a small habit that changes your smartphone from "a tool that tires you out" into "a tool that helps you reset"?

articles.title: Fear of change is just the status quo bias at work. A thought experiment for taking a new step lightly
articles.summary: You are not 100% satisfied with your current environment, but jumping into a new place feels unsettling too, so you end up choosing the same everyday life as always. Have you ever blamed yourself for that, thinking you lack courage...

blocks.text: You are not 100% satisfied with your current environment, but jumping into a new place feels unsettling too, so you end up choosing the same everyday life as always. Have you ever blamed yourself for that, thinking, "I just don't have courage"?
But freezing up in the face of change does not mean you are cowardly. Human beings have a strong instinct called the "status quo bias" — a tendency to prioritize known safety over unknown benefits.
You don't have to leap right away. Start by simulating it in your mind

Trying to force your way through this bias with sheer willpower puts a heavy burden on your mind. What matters is not changing your real-life actions right away, but first trying a thought experiment in a safe place: "What would happen if I chose change?"
The time you spend drawing a card with DECIDE. is exactly that kind of risk-free place for a thought experiment.
Use the "what if" perspective a card gives you as a warm-up for your mind
When you draw a card while wondering about a new option, it presents, in calm words, hints for breaking through your current stuck state, or points you should prepare for in advance.

As you read it, try to build a concrete picture in your mind: "I see — if I prepare in this way, I would probably be okay even if I moved to a new environment." Just doing that mental warm-up can make your fear of change surprisingly smaller.
When you want to break out of the shell of the status quo, instead of forcing yourself to be brave, try starting by quietly drawing a single card.

Bringing the arrow back from "the other person" to "your own stance"

The only way to ease stress in human relationships is to let go of the question "How do I change the other person?" and bring the arrow of your attention back to an area you can control: "What distance and stance should I take toward this person?"

Even if you cannot change the other person, you can shift your own position by half a step, starting today. When you are tired of human relationships, try receiving a thoughtful hint for protecting yourself from the cards.

blocks.text: In modern business and daily life, there is a tendency to treat "instant decisions" as a virtue. When you spend every day being driven — replies should be fast, conclusions should be reached right away — you may start to feel that "the self who still can't decide" is somehow a failure as a person.
But in this world, just as there are things that "should be decided right now," there are also things that "should not be decided yet, but left to mature."
Waiting for the right time is also a fine decision
When you don't have enough information, or when your heart is not yet sorted out, forcing a conclusion out of impatience alone tends to mean you end up having to redo it later.
What matters is not simply putting things off vaguely, but consciously deciding, "For now, I will deliberately not decide, and make this a period for watching how things go."

articles.title: Is "maintaining the status quo" the same as going backward? A small shift in perspective to encourage adults who fear change

The Paradox: The More You Play Defense, the Harder Life Becomes
The more you hide in a shelter out of fear of change, the greater the fear becomes when you eventually have to go out into the world.

articles.title: Turning the fear of "what if I fail?" into energy: a technique for shifting perspective

blocks.text: Whether you're proposing a new project or jumping into a new relationship, the fear — "What if I fail and embarrass myself?" — tightens your chest and makes your legs freeze.
Fear of failure is something everyone has, but if it's too strong, you end up unable to show even half of the ability you should be able to demonstrate.
See Failure Not as an "End Point" but as "Data Collection"
The reason failure is so frightening is that we misunderstand it as "my value as a person has been denied (game over)."

Gain a Calm Perspective and Try Lightly
When you draw a card in DECIDE., even the trouble and anxiety in front of you are reframed in a calm tone as "one passing point" in a long process of growth.

When your mindset shifts to "I'm in a trial-and-error phase right now, so of course I can't do it perfectly yet. In fact, let me gather lots of data," fear naturally disappears and turns into light energy for taking the next step.
Let's graduate from fearing failure, and become adults who lightly enjoy experimenting.

Stop Searching for the Right Path — Resolve to Make Your Chosen Path Right

But no matter how carefully you choose a path, as you go forward you will inevitably hit unexpected walls and difficulties. In other words, in life, there is no such thing as a "right path you can travel from start to finish without getting hurt."

What matters is not so much the difference in the "starting point" of which path you choose, but the "process afterward" — how sincerely you face it after choosing that path, and how you make it right with your own hands.
Walk Your Own Path with a Sense of Conviction as Fuel

The Day When You're 100% Prepared Will Never Come
No matter how thoroughly we think we've prepared, once we actually start moving, unexpected happenings will inevitably occur, and we'll notice things we're missing.

A "moment when all conditions are perfectly in place" is an illusion. The only moment we can move forward is always the imperfect "here and now" — when we can think, "I'm a little anxious, but I've done what I can with who I am now."

When you draw a card in DECIDE., you may encounter a message like, "You're prepared enough — all that's left is to take a step forward."

Break the first step down into its smallest unit

The most effective way to break the habit of procrastination is to break a task down into "the smallest unit that can be finished in 5 minutes." Not "write the proposal," but "open the document and just type in the title." With only that, your brain does not feel threatened.
And when you are unsure what to start with, borrowing an outside viewpoint is the best shortcut.

Open DECIDE., draw one card, and check "the point I should tackle first right now."

The moment a concrete hint appears, such as "First, look over the whole picture" or "Don't worry about the details, just get your hands moving," the heavy reluctance to start putting things off suddenly becomes lighter.

Turn life from a heavy exam into a light experiment

If you can reframe things as "if it doesn't work, I can just try another method," the hurdle to action drops dramatically.
A quiet compass for deciding the direction of your experiment

Let go of the concept of failure, and become an adult who enjoys light experiments.

articles.title: A night to stop worrying about what everyone else is doing, and return to your own center

What matters is not general trends, but firmly having your own yardstick: "What feels comfortable for me right now?"

Time Doing Nothing Is Essential Nourishment for the Heart

articles.title: Living flexibly in an age with no right answers. What it means to have a compass of your own

When you read a message there like "It's time to fully accept what you've achieved so far" or "Now is not the time to force expansion — it's time to solidify your footing," your heart becomes deeply fulfilled: "That's right — I've done enough, so it's okay to feel at ease for a bit."
Why not stop driving yourself, and gently celebrate your own hard work?

articles.title: 'Just get it into shape for now' is what moves a life forward. Practical steps for letting go of perfectionism
